newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Dull Pakistan poll campaign ends with fireworks.
newsitem.headline: Dull Pakistan poll campaign ends with fireworks.

text.p: Pakistan's probable next prime minister, Nawaz Sharif, ended a dull election campaign amid the deafening crack of fireworks in his home city of Lahore on Sunday in what looked like a victory parade.

In stark contrast to the modest crowds drawn by his main opponents in the capital of Pakistan's most populous province, Sharif sent the city's central districts into a frenzy that continued into the early hours despite steady rain.

Ousted prime minister Benazir Bhutto, whose dismissal by President Farooq Leghari on disputed corruption charges on November 5 forced elections two years early, drew only a few thousand people to her rallies on Saturday, the last day of campaigning before Monday's vote.
Imran Khan, the former Pakistani cricket captain who is a national hero, drew an even more modest crowd to his final rally in Lahore, where he lives.

Imran's audience reacted enthusiastically to his appeal to elect honest politicians who would end rampant corruption, but political analysts say his Tehrik-i-Insaaf (Justice Movement) is unlikely to win more than handful of seats, if any.

Sharif, a handkerchief frequently held to his mouth against the dense and acrid smoke from fireworks set off by exuberant supporters, brought the first real excitement to an election campaign marked by apathy.
Women threw rose petals from balconies onto his open-topped vehicle as it wound through the narrow muddy streets of central Lahore, where he is a candidate.
Thousands of people, mostly young men, thronged the streets, hundreds of them following the motorcade and frequently bringing it to halt as they pressed against Sharif's car, hoping to touch him.
Sharif ended his tortuous journey through the city with a well-attended rally that outshone anything his rivals had produced.
Sharif, an industrialist whose victory would please stock markets which have revived as his election prospects blossomed, has been prime minister before.

He was dismissed on corruption charges, but the order was reversed by the Supreme Court and his government was restored briefly before losing elections to Bhutto's Pakistan People's Party (PPP) in October 1993.
Last week, the Supreme Court upheld Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto, saying there was enough evidence of corruption and nepotism to justify sacking her.

A bitter Bhutto has hinted that she might not accept the election results if the PPP is beaten, saying her dismissal was part of a plot to drive the PPP out of politics, and accusing Leghari, a former close ally, of trying to form a "king's party" to perpetuate himself in power.
She has alleged that Leghari has done a deal with Sharif to allow the PML leader into power as part of the plot. Both men deny the charge.
Most political analysts say the PML will emerge the biggest part in the 217-seat National Assembly, but fall short of a majority.

That view was backed on Sunday by a survey by the English-language daily The News, which predicted that the PML would win 79 seats, the PPP and its allies 46, with the rest scattered among small parties and independents.

It said around 12 seats would go to the Mohajir National Movement (MQM) based in the southern city of Karachi. The MQM represents Urdu-speakers who crossed from India to Pakistan when the old British Raj was partitioned on Independence in 1947.
The MQM's campaign against what it calls anti-Mohajir discrimination has sparked years of violence in Karachi, Pakistan's commercial capital, in which thousands of people have been killed.

Bhutto, speaking in Lahore on Saturday, took credit for ending what she called terrorism in Karachi. Most analysts say the MQM is likely to throw its weight behind the pro-business Sharif if the PML does not win an overall majority.
